A single, specific idea that couldn't belong to any other piece: a flat black silhouette of an ad man falls past skyscraper glass that reflects period advertising. It works as a visual metaphor for the character's collapse into his own industry.
Graphic Saul Bass-style silhouettes are set against photographic collage. Mixing those two textures is a deliberate choice of method, not a default.

The choreography has a clear arc: a man enters an office, a close-up of shoes, the fall through layered ad imagery, and a resolution where he sits back on the couch with a cigarette. The calm ending reframes the whole fall.
Varied shot scale and angle (wide, extreme close-up, tumbling top-down, mid shot) show real camera thinking.
Restrained palette of black, warm grey, period red and the faded colours of the ads; the red/black split in the title type echoes the red in the ad imagery.
The typography is simple, but its placement leaves room for the figure, and the two-colour name treatment is consistent and on period.
gaps: The credit typography is functional rather than expressive. A more period-specific face, or type that interacts with the falling figure, could raise it further.
The ad-collage layers are sometimes busy enough to blur the silhouette's read in the middle of the fall. Tighter control of layer contrast would sharpen those frames.
Light is mostly flat by design. A little more atmospheric depth in the glass reflections would add richness without breaking the graphic language.

tells: The central idea is the world as a clockwork map: cities wind up out of the map like mechanical models. It's specific to the story, structural, and doubles as an atlas for the viewer.

Rich physical materials: tarnished brass, carved wood, engraved metal bands, parchment. Lighting is motivated by a central sun source, with lens bloom and shallow depth of field that give the models miniature scale.
Credits are set in a carved serif with small heraldic sigils beside each name, so the type is tied to the world's iconography rather than laid over it.
Shot variety: macro on the engraved astrolabe band, low-angle fly-overs of the mechanisms, a top-down map with a pin line, and a closing emblem lockup that bookends the sun-glow opening.
A coherent warm sepia/bronze palette with deep shadow; every frame holds up as a poster.
gaps: The title lockup in the last frame is more conventional and 'epic-trailer' than the mechanical idea deserves; it could come out of the clockwork itself.
The flat map frame is visually weaker than the mechanical frames and loses some of the material density.
The palette is almost monochrome bronze. A sharper colour shift per region would strengthen the sense of moving between places.

tells: Typography is the subject: custom fragmented letterforms, Latin and katakana glyphs broken into modular strokes, and dot-matrix/pixel-grid lettering. The type has a clear system and a point of view.
A deliberate, unusual palette (hot pink, cyan, acid lime, violet, signal red on near-black) used with discipline from frame to frame.

Layouts change radically from frame to frame (a large cropped D with a target, horizontal bands, a framed glyph field, a diagonal shard, a pixel grid, a dense collage), which suggests varied choreography, not a repeated slide.
Fine print texture, scanline and grain detail, plus layered UI-like ornament that reads as designed, not placeholder.
Frames are dense and layered, with real figure/ground play between type and graphic shapes.
gaps: The idea leans on a familiar 'cyber Tokyo glitch typography' genre. It needs a more specific concept than the aesthetic itself to match A's single, memorable metaphor.
There's no physical light or material depth; adding print, paper or projected-light texture would give the frames weight like B has.
Legibility of the payoff (the 'TOKYO' frame) gets lost in the collage. A clearer moment of resolution would give the motion a climax.

tells: One specific idea: a silhouetted man falls past skyscraper windows that carry period advertising. The fall stands for the character's inner collapse, and it is tied closely to the show's world.
A deliberate limited palette: flat black silhouettes against muted cream interiors, with saturated vintage ad imagery reflected in the glass grid.

The camera moves through a clear sequence of scales: wide office, close-up shoes, the fall at several sizes, then the reclined pose at the end that resolves it. That is real choreography with a beginning and an end.
The type is restrained but considered. A two-weight caps credit with a red first name repeats across frames as a system and leaves room for the image.
The silhouette-on-ad layering and the final frame rhyme with Saul Bass and are instantly recognisable. Each frame works as a poster.
gaps: The typography is deliberately quiet. The credits sit on the image rather than interacting with it, so the type is not as expressive as it could be.
Light is mostly flat and graphic by design. There is little atmospheric depth outside the ad reflections.
The interior layout in the first frame is plainer and more diagrammatic than the later layered frames.

tells: The concept is a clockwork map whose mechanical cities build themselves. It works as a world-building device and as an orientation tool, and only this show could have it.
The material work is very rich: engraved brass, bone-white spires, weathered wood and parchment terrain, with real directional light, lens flare from the astrolabe sun, and depth of field.
Scale and camera vary: a macro on the engraved band, low-angle tabletop shots of mechanical cities, then a top-down map, all resolving into a lockup that mirrors the opening frame.
Credits are set in a period serif with small house sigils, built into each shot's composition.
Warm amber and gold against cool slate is a consistent, motivated palette.
gaps: The credit typography is conventional, a classic engraved-style serif. Its legibility suffers over busy textures, as in the 'Oral Norrie Ottey' frame.
The flat top-down map frame has less material depth than the 3D mechanism shots.
The final logo lockup with radial glow is closer to genre convention than to the surprise of the mechanisms.

tells: The typographic idea runs through the whole piece: Latin and katakana glyphs are broken into modular parts that scatter, rotate and reassemble into 'TOKYO'. The type is the subject, not a label.
The palette is unusual and deliberate (hot pink, cyan, acid lime, violet on aubergine-black), and it changes from frame to frame without losing coherence.
Compositions vary a lot: bold close-up crop, horizontal band, framed glyph field, diagonal scatter, dot-matrix grid, dense collage. This is not one layout with swapped words.
The layers are dense: halftone, scanline and pixel textures, plus pixel-grid glyphs that suggest a city-signage or transit-display reference.
gaps: The glitch and dot-matrix vocabulary is a well-worn genre. It needs an observation more specific to its subject to reach the singular concept of A.
There is no real light or material depth. Texture is surface grain and pixel overlay rather than a sense of space or substance.
The last frame is so busy that the final 'TOKYO' reveal loses hierarchy. It needs a cleaner payoff to match A's resolved last image.

defects: The wings are flat rigid cards hinged at the shoulder. There is no feather articulation, overlap or follow-through, and the flap reads as a rotating rectangle.
The wing motion blur is a stepped frame-blend smear, with ghost copies visible at the wing edges, not true shutter blur. At the 100% crop the edge of the blurred wing is a hard diagonal line.
The bird is a low-detail primitive: smooth silhouette, rim light only on the head, and a hard dark tail fin with no feathers.
Heavy uniform luminance noise covers the whole frame at 100% and buries detail. It reads as grain applied to hide banding, not as a filmic grain response.
The wordmark is held for about 2 s and the final shot runs 5.0 s. The grass and drifting specks move, but the type does nothing after it lands, so this is dead air.
The 'kestrel.' shadow and reflection on the grass are a smeared, doubled projection that does not match the low backlight. The letter bases do not seat into the grass convincingly.
The opening frames are an out-of-focus wing filling the frame, with an unclear subject and composition.

The audio is plainly synthetic: a regular noise pulse at about 7 Hz for the wingbeats, one filtered-noise swell for the dive, then a static drone with three sine chirps (harmonic stacks) for the call. There is no music bed or texture layering.
gaps: Creature animation: a top studio would give a real hover-and-stoop cycle, with wing overlap, primary feathers bending, tail correction and head stabilisation, and the dive would accelerate with weight. Here the bird flaps a hinged card at a constant rate and the transition from the dive to the dot is abrupt.

The bird-to-full-stop payoff needs a built hand-off: track the falling dot, make an impact or settle on the period, and have the grass react. As it stands the dot is a tiny element that jump-cuts to the finished wordmark, which then sits static for about 2 s with no secondary animation and no rhyme with the opening shot.

Sound and finish: the wingbeat noise pulses, dive swell and sine chirps sync to picture but are thin and generated, with no low-end weight, room or produced score. The image relies on blanket noise and frame-blended smears where it needs real motion blur, depth of field, feather texture and an integrated type contact shadow.
